name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Trash fish? More like some of the oldest — and important — species in Minnesota
description: Casting along a drop-off on the St. Croix River, I felt some sharp tugs. I thought this might be rocks or clams. But then the pole bent hard toward the water. The line took off, circling. I fought to reel the fish up and in until I finally got it to the boat. “That’s a […]
text:
Solomon David, a University of Minneota scientist who studies the ancient and often overlooked native fish of the Mississippi River Basin, holds a shortnose gar, at an inland Minnesota lake. (Photo courtesy of the GarLab)Casting along a drop-off on the St. Croix River, I felt some sharp tugs. I thought this might be rocks or clams. But then the pole bent hard toward the water. The line took off, circling. I fought to reel the fish up and in until I finally got it to the boat.
“That’s a nice drum!” said Tyler Winter. “They get bigger than that. But not a lot.”
 It was 18.5 inches. 
We raced back up to Stillwater for the awards ceremony. Winter is the director of Native Fish for Tomorrow, and we were at the 78th annual Governor’s Fishing Opener. For the first time since fishing regulations began, an entire class of neglected species were being formally, publicly recognized.
The day before, May 8, Gov. Tim Walz had signed a proclamation declaring the first ever “Native Fish Day.” This was not just about walleye, bass and crappie. Native Fish Day was meant to celebrate the 26 other native species that have been here for thousands, if not millions, of years: redhorse, quillback, suckers, gar, bowfin and buffalo. The last of these is often mistaken for carp. But buffalo is not a carp. We’ll get to that later. 
Until recently, little was known about any of these fish. But thanks to the pioneering work of Alec Lackmann at the University of Minnesota, Duluth, we’ve learned that bigmouth buffalo, for instance, can live to more than 100 years. In Canada, he found one that was 148. Some buffalo alive today were born in the 1800s. They’re the 11th longest lived vertebrate in the world, and are likely the oldest living animal in North America.
Until recently, these species were all classified as “rough fish,” or “trash fish.” None of them had limits or protections, and due to an outdated, frontier mentality toward wildlife in the water, they could be killed en masse with no consequences.
But in 2024, Minnesota passed the “Native Fish Bill,” becoming the first state in the nation to grant these species a modicum of protection. Now, at the Governor’s Fishing Opener, they were being honored another way: Instead of one competition for the biggest walleye, there were two: One for walleye and one for drum, a native species that can live more than 50 years, eats vast amounts of invasive zebra mussels, and which many say is as good to eat as walleye.
As we made our way back to Stillwater, in my mind I’d already caught the biggest drum. I was mentally spending my $100, flaunting my “Native Fish For Tomorrow” hat and admiring my drum trophy — the first one awarded in 150 years of fish management. 
Sadly, when we got back, I learned that another fisherman named Tim Smith had caught a 22-inch drum. 
“I grew up along the Mississippi,” Smith told me at the awards ceremony. “And I don’t know if I would have known what that was. I probably would have called it a carp.”
We call a lot of fish carp. They are not carp.
A drum is not a carp. But Smith is far from alone. It’s mindboggling how people can know so much about walleye or trout, but so little about, say, white sucker, which is one of the most ecologically important fish in the state. 
Bigmouth buffalo, left, and common carp, two fish separated by 50 million years of evolution. (Photo by Frank Bures/Minnesota Reformer)
It speaks to our general underwater ignorance. Common carp were imported from Germany in 1877 by the federal government and sent across the U.S for stocking. By the time they realized this was a mistake, it was too late: Carp were everywhere. Removal began in the early 1900s and continues today. 
After that, any fish people didn’t care to catch, including carp, were called “rough fish.” Still today, many fishermen call anything that’s not a “game fish” a carp. That includes redhorse, quillback, drum and many others. None of these fish are carp. 
Even the poorly named “carpsucker” is not a carp.
Buffalo are often called “buffalo carp.” 
They are not carp. Buffalo and carp are separated by 50 million years of evolution. There are five kinds of buffalo, three of which (bigmouth, smallmouth and black) are native to Minnesota. “Kandiyohi,” as the central Minnesota county is called, is Dakota for “where the buffalo fish come.” 
We’ve also learned that in some waterways, bigmouth buffalo have not successfully reproduced for more than 80 years. The individuals in those waters were born in the 1920s, 1930s or as late as the 1950s. But almost none after that. 
No one knows why. This is because there’s been no funding for, or even much interest in, researching “rough fish.” Instead, it was considered good practice to wipe them out to make room for more desirable species like walleye, bass and pike.
That began to change in 2021 with the publication of a paper in the scientific journal Fisheries titled: “Goodbye to ‘Rough Fish’: Paradigm Shift in the Conservation of Native Fishes.” The authors, including the University of Minnesota’s gar specialist Solomon David, argued that native fish deliver critical “ecosystem services,” and that they are “long-lived and vulnerable to overfishing and decline.” 
Around the same time the paper was published, a video went viral of ice fisherman on the Minnesota River spearing 82 gar — the ancient, long-nosed, air-breathing fish — and leaving them on the ice to die.
The incident prompted state government to impose a 10-gar possession limit in 2023 — the first-ever such protection. Later that year, the “No Junk Fish” bill passed the Minnesota Legislature, requiring research on the conservation status of all native fish. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Then in April 2024, the landmark “Native Fish Bill” was signed by Walz. This changed 41 statutes to protect these species and to separate them from common carp. It also laid the groundwork for research and protections of the 26 “native rough fish.” After the bill passed, carp were re-classified as a “regulated invasive species,” and there was now no such thing as a “rough fish” in Minnesota.
These fish are currently subject to Minnesota’s “wanton waste” law, which states that, “a person may not wantonly waste or destroy a usable part of a protected wild animal,” and that it, “does not apply to common carp.” 
The wanton waste law is rarely enforced. But now the Department of Natural Resources is proposing limits ranging from 5 to 30 for these native fish. Thirty seems like a lot, but it’s better than nothing. 
Most significantly, though, the Native Fish Bill marked a growing recognition that these fish belong here and have value. (The drum, for example, is host to 11 species of native mussels.) 
At the Governor’s Fishing Opener, I talked to a sixth-grade girl named Lucile who was excited to catch these fish for the first time.
“I caught a walleye, a perch, a drum, a silver head redhorse and a shorthead redhorse,” she told me.
“Do you think you’ll want to catch more of those?” I asked
“Yeah, definitely,” she said. “I like catching new fish that are cool and interesting to me.”
 Amid the bowfishers, who love these species
Another group also loves catching those fish: Bowfishers. 
Over the past two decades, bowfishing has exploded in popularity. The sport uses arrows with a line attached to hunt fish at night. Their boats are equipped with light bars shining thousands of watts into the water, spotting and disorienting the fish. 
Bowfishing in itself is not a problem, but its meteoric rise in popularity, and the growth of tournaments, has fueled concerns about the impact on native fish populations. 
Vern Bachmann, 40, has been bowfishing since he was a kid. But over the past two decades, he’s grown concerned. 
“When I first got into shooting buffalo, they were everywhere,” he said. “We could literally put the boat in drive and let it go wherever it wanted. And there were hundreds upon hundreds of fish everywhere. Nowadays, you’re lucky to see 10 fish a night.”
As the sport got bigger, Bachmann quit going to tournaments. His little jon boat couldn’t compete with the $50,000 rigs that were showing up. When he used to go out at night, he would be the only one. Today it’s practically guaranteed there will be a couple others out. He still goes occasionally, but he’s increasingly selective about what he shoots. 
“It definitely makes you think twice when you’re shooting a fish that’s older than your grandparents. That fish survived for a 100 years, and now you’re just throwing it in the weeds. It’s like….what a waste. We’re literally wiping them out of existence.”
Ryan Barthel is president of the Land of Lakes Bowfishing Association, and host of the Big 10 Battle tournament.
When I asked him about the impending restrictions, he said: “I personally don’t agree with it. That’s just my opinion. I feel they don’t have the facts. They have no statistics showing that what we’re doing is having any impact on the population.”
No one has data because this kind of research hasn’t been funded yet. But Barthel says in his experience, there are still plenty of fish. 
“I’m on the water from one to six days a week, either scouting for myself, guiding or in tournaments,” he told me. “I see a lot of lakes, a lot of water, and the amount of fish of all species you see is just incredible. On lakes that I know get fished really hard with a lot of people, I’m still seeing 5,000 fish a night.
Barthel also said bowfishing helps “clean up people’s lakes and make them better for the game fish.” But whether the sport is reducing nongame fish populations, or having no impact at all, will need to be established by research. But in places where bowfishing has eradicated common carp, degraded lakes can bounce back. 
“Mud Lake by Perham used to be absolutely full of carp,” Bachman told me. “Well, now that we pretty much got the carp eliminated there, the wild rice has come back thicker than thick and it’s fabulous for duck hunting.”
If bowfishing were limited to carp, it would be a genuine service. Every year, millions of dollars are spent across the state on carp removal. 
I asked Barthel if he’d be open to running a carp-only tournament. 
“I wouldn’t be opposed to that,” he said. “I’d rather it not come to that, but if that’s what it comes to, that’s what we’ll have to do.”
At the moment, however, that’s not the case.
The volume of fish killed at bowfishing tournaments is massive. At the 2026 AMS Bowfishing “Big 20 Challenge,” in Stratford, Wisconsin, 61 teams registered over 27,000 pounds of fish. The winning team’s top 20 take was 668 pounds — over 30 pounds per fish. 
The total weight registered is far from all the fish caught. Smaller fish go straight in the dumpster because they don’t make the top 20. That means the true measure of the take at the AMS tournament was far more than what the scale showed. 
And while many of those fish are carp (the tournaments don’t record numbers, so it’s impossible to know), AMS also awarded prizes for the biggest quillback (10.2 pounds, $1000); drum (12 pounds, prize unknown); gar (12.8 pounds, $500); bowfin (8.4 pounds, prize — a new bow); and buffalo (47.2 pounds, $1,700). 
Over two tons of fish ready to be hauled away after a fishing tournament, brought to an organic soil company and made into fertilizer. (Photo by Frank Bures/Minnesota Reformer)
Wisconsin has no limits for any of these native fish, so this is all legal. 
In Minnesota, however, that will soon change, which is why the Land of Lakes Bowfishing Association circulated a petition this spring for a hearing on the new laws. In it, they stated they were “opposed to the current adoption of limits on native rough fish,” because “The Minnesota DNR … clearly states the population status of many of these species is not understood,” and that when the new regulations went into effect, “native rough fish would have to be cleaned and consumed,” among other objections.
The Big 10 Battle
I decided I needed to see one of these tournaments for myself. So I headed north to Sauk Centre, where Barthel’s 10th annual “Big 10 Battle” was taking place. 
The sky was turning red as the first trucks rolled in, airboats in tow, after a long night of prowling rivers and lakes. The weigh-in was at the Stearns County Fairgrounds.
Once I saw people standing on boats, throwing fish into a dumpster that didn’t make their top 10, I headed over. (Only the 10 biggest fish are weighed for the contest.)  
The cutoff time was 7 a.m. By then, 22 of the 38 teams had made it back to the fairgrounds. The night had been cold and windy, so a few guys stood shivering in their rubber boots and camouflage. 
I wandered around to look at the boats. They were long and flat, with platforms for standing high over the water. On the front were mounted light bars to shine on the fish. Some had “airboat” fans so they could push the fish into the shallows where they’re breeding. It’s an arms race the fish can’t win. 
Each team put its biggest 10 fish in the trash can on the scale. Once the weight was recorded, the fish were tipped into the dumpster. (After the tournament, the fish would be hauled to an organic soil company in town and made into fertilizer.) I peered over the edge and could see it was filling fast. Most of the fish were dead, but a few lay gasping. Many were carp, but there were a few bowfins, buffalo and gar mixed in.    
As the later teams arrived, the number of “big buffs” went up. I watched one team put five bigmouth buffalo on the scale — all pregnant females — which weighed over 160 pounds. Based on their size, they would likely have been between 90 and 100 years old. After they were tipped into the dumpster, a wash of their eggs poured over them.    
Fish by fish, the dumpster filled. I tried to take photos discreetly. (Most bowfishing groups in Minnesota have quit posting trophy photos.) But it was a public grounds and fish are a public resource. 
There was one massive fish I didn’t recognize, until someone mentioned that it was a drum. It was many, many times bigger than the one I’d caught at the Governor’s Fishing Opener. Another person said it was probably bigger than the state record (35 pounds) but we’ll never know. It went into the dumpster with the rest. 
The author with his runner-up drum. (Courtesy photo)
In the end, team “Carpnado” were declared the winners, with 10 fish totaling 317 pounds. They were followed by “Swamp Donkey Outdoors” at 299 pounds and “Back Roads Archery” at 287.  There was also a prize for the biggest common carp, which clocked in at 47 pounds. 
No prizes were given for any native species. 
The total combined weight of all the teams was just under 4,500 pounds. If you’d included each teams’ non-top 10 fish, the total would have been a lot more. But, it was far less than the AMS tournament in Wisconsin.
After the awards were given out, I heard raised voices and wandered over to see what the argument was about. It turned out three teams had been disqualified for not removing their drain plugs while transporting their boats. (The “drain plug law” is aimed at stopping the spread of zebra mussels.)
“Can you show where it says in the rules you’re not allowed to do that?” said an exasperated young man.
“It’s in the DNR book,” another answered. “If you don’t follow Minnesota state law, you’re out.”
The man threw up his hands and walked away. 
And with that, the Big 10 Battle was over. The teams had already started to leave. 
On my way out, I approached an older woman who I’d seen at the weigh-in table.
“Are you guys going to do this again next year?” I asked.
“Oh yeah!” she said, “This is our 10th year.”
Her tone was confident, as if it was a silly question.
And maybe it was. Maybe she was right. Maybe there would always be more of these fish. Maybe the buffalo would bounce back. Maybe the bowfishing bonanza would never end. 
Or maybe, more hopefully, the sport would do what native fish have done to survive.
Maybe it would evolve.

name: California
title: CA Democrats want election results faster, but say any solution hurts voters
description: California’s slow vote count garnered national attention in the days following the June 2 primary — raising familiar questions about what can be done to speed up the tally. And while both state Democrats and Republicans say they would like results to be finalized faster, Democratic leaders aren’t likely to implement serious changes if it […]
text:
A ballot processor organizes mail-in ballots at the Sacramento County Voter Registration and Elections office in Sacramento on June 2, 2026. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters




California’s slow vote count garnered national attention in the days following the June 2 primary — raising familiar questions about what can be done to speed up the tally. And while both state Democrats and Republicans say they would like results to be finalized faster, Democratic leaders aren’t likely to implement serious changes if it means disenfranchising voters in the process.
As CalMatters’ Maya C. Miller explains, it took about a week for enough ballots to be counted to call the California governor’s race. During that time, the vote count drew criticism from President Donald Trump, the popular election-data analyst Nate Silver and The New York Times’ editorial board, which contended that California’s delayed results were “damaging faith in government.”
State Democratic leaders say that because the slow count is mostly due to the high volume of mail-in ballots that come in on Election Day or the day before, speeding up the count could make voting harder for some Californians.

Assemblymember Gail Pellerin, a Santa Cruz Democrat, chairperson of the election committee and former county registrar: “If you want results election night, you’re going to have to go back to in-person voting, way earlier deadlines for returning by mail and you’re going to end up disenfranchising voters.”

California’s secretary of state, Shirley Weber, also dismissed concerns about slow returns as a Trump talking point: “For me, accuracy is far more important,” Weber told CalMatters in April.
Mail-in ballots also require more time, labor and money to process compared to in-person ballots. But California counties do not receive enough funding to pay for more workers, according to the Public Policy Institute of California. Unlike some other states, California also does not contribute ongoing funds to counties for elections.

Eric McGhee, a senior fellow at the PPIC, in regards to county registrars: “They’re kind of managing the best they can with the budget that they have. But it’s a lot to handle.”

Read more.



As AI becomes a frontline tool in healthcare, what comes next? Join us Wednesday in Sacramento at the UC Student and Policy Center for a conversation on guardrails, patient care and innovation in healthcare. Register here.

Other Stories You Should Know


Taxes as a lifeline for CA healthcare?


Signs reading “A Billionaire Tax Now” at a rally in Los Angeles on Feb. 18, 2026. Photo by Jason Armond, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images




A major California union and lawmakers are advancing two separate tax proposals to offset sweeping federal cuts to Medicaid that congressional Republicans approved through their 2025 spending bill and Trump signed into law.
The first proposal, backed by the state’s largest healthcare workers union, qualified for the November ballot last week. It would levy a one-time, 5% tax on the state’s billionaires, which proponents say would generate $100 billion for the state. Gov. Gavin Newsom, healthcare industry groups and California’s wealthy tech executives oppose the measure. The California Teachers Association also opposes it, putting forward its own ballot initiative to make permanent an existing surtax on wealthy Californians.
A second proposal approved by the Legislature would restructure the state’s managed care organization tax in a way that would shift more cost onto privately insured Californians. One health insurance lobby estimated that the change could result in consumers paying about $100 more in premiums each year.
Read more about the billionaire tax and MCO tax proposals from CalMatters’ Kristen Hwang and Ana B. Ibarra, respectively.



Cal State and union clash over AI


A student walks up the stairs at the Innovation and Instruction building at Cal State Dominguez Hills in Carson on Feb. 19, 2026. Photo by Zin Chiang for CalMatters




A bill that would ban California State University from replacing faculty with generative artificial intelligence tools highlights the growing tension between the university system and its faculty over Cal State’s use of AI, writes CalMatters’ Mikhail Zinshteyn.
Though few examples exist of Cal State attempting to replace faculty labor with AI, the role of the technology more broadly has sown fears among members of the California Faculty Association, the union of professors backing the bill.
In 2025, the union filed an unfair labor practices complaint against Sacramento State, accusing its then-chief AI officer, Alexander Sidorkin, of soliciting faculty for their course materials “to receive a customized AI tutoring bot for their classes.” The union also alleged that Sidorkin created a mental health chatbot for students, and linked the bot on a resources webpage. Cal State officials denied this.
The union ultimately withdrew its complaint after Cal State and the union settled the overall matter in March. Sidorkin, who had no knowledge that he was named in the complaint until CalMatters reached out to him, said he never created a bot. Rather, he wanted to recommend that students use ChatGPT during a mental health episode if counselors weren’t available.
Read more.



And lastly: ‘Minor tweaks’ spark major backlash


Assemblymember Blanca Pacheco speaks with a fellow lawmaker at the state Capitol in Sacramento on June 13, 2024. Photo by Cristian Gonzalez for CalMatters




To get proposed legislation out of the Assembly, Assemblymember Blanca Pacheco watered down a controversial bill that would reduce access to public records. Now the Downey Democrat has brought the contentious elements back, and they’re more restrictive than before. It’s “a virtual horror show of governmental nontransparency,” said one transparency advocate about Pacheco’s measure. Read more from CalMatters’ Yue Stella Yu.






California Voices
CalMatters columnist Dan Walters: Raising minimum wages to offset California’s rising living costs can lead to higher consumer costs, which then increases pressure for higher wages and pushes those caught in the middle to lower-cost states.
Deteriorating environmental conditions, droughts and proposed solar and mining projects threaten the Mojave Desert’s Joshua trees — potentially affecting the local economy that surrounds Joshua Tree National Park, writes Jacob Mull, a graduate student studying conservation leadership at Colorado State University.
California political and philanthropic leaders must do more to help preserve Black communities and histories so that they can withstand shifting political climates that are opposed to preserving Black spaces, writes Kaci Patterson, founder and chief architect of the Black Equity Collective.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: MUSC opens emergency-urgent care hybrid in Lower Richland, a first of its kind for SC
description: Residents of rural Lower Richland now have access to emergency healthcare close to home, thanks to SC’s state-owned hospital system.
text:
Medical University of South Carolina President Dr. David Cole, right, shakes hands with Richland County Coroner Naida Rutherford at MUSC Health's new hybrid emergency-urgent care clinic in Lower Richland. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Residents of rural Richland County now have access to emergency healthcare close to home, thanks to South Carolina’s state-owned hospital system.
The Medical University of South Carolina Health system partnered with a Texas-based company to build a 12,484-square-foot hybrid emergency room and urgent care for the region southeast of Columbia known as Lower Richland.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The center’s opening Monday marks an answer to pleas that began more than three decades ago from state Sen. Darrell Jackson and the late Rep. Joe Neal, both Hopkins Democrats and pastors first elected to the Statehouse in 1992. Neal, a beloved champion of the needy, died unexpectedly in 2017 at a Columbia hospital.
Richland County legislators’ ask, Jackson said, was for some kind of emergency healthcare for the community, if not a full-fledged hospital.
“If someone is having a health emergency, they should not have to go all the way into Columbia to do that,” Jackson said.
Officials with MUSC and its partner believe the Lower Richland facility is the first of its kind in the state, but it won’t be the only one they build. Plans are underway for combined centers in Florence, Summerville and West Ashley.
Intuitive Health, the Texas company, also is working with Tidelands Health to build three sites in Horry County and with Beaufort Memorial to bring one to the southern end of Hilton Head Island.
In addition to expanding access, it can also save people money, the partners say. If someone comes in unsure whether they need emergency level care, they’re only billed for the level of care they actually receive.
“It solves a common patient problem: Where should I go?” said Dr. David Cole, president of the MUSC medical school. “If you go to the wrong place, you’ll get significant charge differentials. When you come here, you don’t worry about that.”
The CT scanner at MUSC Health’s new hybrid emergency-urgent care clinic in Lower Richland. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)
Unlike a typical urgent care, the new center is equipped with high-tech medical imaging, including computed tomography (commonly called a CT scan) that combines X-rays with computer technology to create detailed images, as well as ultrasounds and electrocardiogram machines.
It also has a fully equipped trauma bay. So, if someone gets in a car wreck, is having a baby, a stroke or a heart attack, the center’s physicians can at least get them stabilized until they’re well enough to be transported to one of the area’s larger hospitals for admission.
Founded by an emergency room doctor, it’s a model Intuitive has been following since 2008.
With the addition of South Carolina, the company will have more than 35 centers across 11 states. Arizona, Delaware, Florida, Kentucky, Indiana, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas, Virginia and Washington are the others.
“It takes the guesswork out of the hands of the patients,” said Marshall Leslie, the chief growth officer for Intuitive. “If they don’t need emergency level services, they go home with a simple urgent care bill.”
Cindy Little, the new center’s nurse manager, said she’s seen it in her personal life. She’s been dehydrated, suspecting a saline drip at an urgent care would probably be enough but not knowing for sure. And she’s had a family member go to the urgent care expecting the nurses to patch up a cut that actually ended up requiring a trip to the emergency room for stitches.
The trauma bay at MUSC Health’s new hybrid emergency-urgent care clinic in Lower Richland. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)
There are three other urgent care centers — one operated by Prisma Health, one by Novant Health and one by HCA Healthcare — within one square mile of the new MUSC building.
“We appreciate some of the urgent care facilities, but no one was willing to do a 24-hour, seven-days-a-week facility,” Sen. Jackson said. “That is what makes this a game changer.”
Richland County Coroner Naida Rutherford provided details about the community’s great need.
If you live around the towns of Hopkins or Eastover, she said, “you have a higher likelihood of death because you could not access emergency care services in a timely manner.”
Since she took office in 2021 through the end of 2023, Rutherford counted the deaths she responded to in those town’s zip codes: 28 in total “from a child who was having an asthma attack to a woman who died on a day that should have been the happiest day of her life, her due date.”
“If you live in rural South Carolina, you should not die because you don’t have access to emergency services,” Rutherford said.
MUSC Health has been considering opening this type of facility in the state since before the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, said Dr. Patrick Cawley, the state hospital system’s CEO. But when the virus hit South Carolina, overwhelming nursing rooms and blowing hospitals’ budgets, it put those plans on pause.
When the hospital system finally recovered and could restart those discussions, it turned to Intuitive for its know-how in developing and operating these complicated centers. Intuitive will take care of day-to-day operations. The two will equally split ownership.
And though MUSC is state-owned, Jackson said no taxpayer dollars went into building the center. It was financed by the partners and will be paid for by the revenue it generates.
The X-ray machine at MUSC Health’s new hybrid emergency-urgent care clinic in Lower Richland. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)
Cawley also said MUSC knew it wanted a location in the Columbia area as part of the effort.
To sell the hospital system on Lower Richland, Rep. Jermaine Johnson took Cawley and other administrators on a tour.
“I got them to come to my house, and I put them in my car, and I drove them around,” said the Hopkins Democrat who’s represented parts of Lower Richland since 2020. “I showed them the community. I showed them the development. I showed them the things that were happening here.”
“I was surprised,” Cawley said. “You look at the numbers on a spreadsheet, and you think, well, there’s some healthcare here within a certain distance. But when you start driving around, you realize there’s not as much as there needs to be.”
“This is a growing area,” Cawley added. “So, we think it’s the perfect community for this kind of access.”
In addition to the Lower Richland center, MUSC has been investing in its other Columbia-area facilities, too.
Since the state-owned hospital purchased the former Providence Health, Cawley said it has gone from having a lot of empty beds to jammed full, to the point they’re building a new emergency room and considering adding another tower of rooms to the downtown Columbia hospital.

name: Delaware
title: Friday’s BeVisionary singles night gives Delaware men over 50 a different reason to get out
description: Women’s tickets are nearly sold out for Friday’s Wilmington event, but men’s tickets remain available WILMINGTON — For single men over 50 who are tired of dating apps, awkward introductions or feeling like they are starting over alone, a Wilmington event this week is being pitched as something different: a night out built around conversation, comfort and rea[...]
text:
BeVisionary host age specific single events for people tried of dating apps. The leader in these events is hosting their next Delaware event on Friday June 26th.
Women’s tickets are nearly sold out for Friday’s Wilmington event, but men’s tickets remain available
WILMINGTON — For single men over 50 who are tired of dating apps, awkward introductions or feeling like they are starting over alone, a Wilmington event this week is being pitched as something different: a night out built around conversation, comfort and real-life connection.
BeVisionary will host Wilmington Singles Night for ages 50 and older from 7 to 10 p.m. Friday, June 26, at HomeBase Delaware, 4723 Concord Pike.
Organizers say women’s tickets are nearly sold out, while tickets for men remain available.
That imbalance is part of what makes the event timely. Many men in their 50s, 60s and beyond say they want companionship, conversation and a reason to get out, but they are less enthusiastic about traditional dating events or online dating. BeVisionary’s approach is designed to lower that barrier by creating a curated social room rather than a high-pressure dating environment.
The event includes a live DJ, conversation starters and a room of singles in the same general stage of life. Tickets are $25 for one person or $40 for a “You + Single Guy Friend” option, giving men a chance to attend with a buddy instead of walking in alone.
The company describes its format as connection first, dating second. That distinction may matter most for men who have been divorced, widowed or simply out of the dating scene for years. Rather than speed dating, forced introductions or a spotlight moment, the evening is structured more like a social mixer with a purpose.
For many men over 50, the hardest part of dating is not interest. It is the first step.
BeVisionary’s model tries to answer the concerns that often keep men home: not wanting to feel judged, not wanting to look desperate, not knowing what to say and not wanting to be the only man in the room. The Wilmington event offers an age-matched setting, a professional host and a clear social format meant to make mingling easier.
The event also comes at a time when many adults are looking for alternatives to online dating. BeVisionary’s concept is based on the idea that people still want to meet in person, but need better places to do it. The group’s events are built around music, energy, conversation and a curated crowd, with the goal of making meeting someone feel natural instead of transactional.
For Delaware men over 50, Friday’s event may be less about “dating” and more about re-entering a social world that can become smaller with age, work changes, divorce, retirement or loss. The promise is simple: show up, have a drink, hear some music, talk to people and see what happens.
And with women’s tickets nearly gone, organizers are making a direct appeal to men: the room is waiting.

When: 7 to 10 p.m. Friday, June 26
Where: HomeBase Delaware, 4723 Concord Pike, Wilmington
Tickets: $25 solo; $40 for “You + Single Guy Friend”  Wilmington Singles Night 50+ | BeVisionary
What’s included: Live DJ, social starters, curated room of singles 50 and older and complimentary matchmaking membership

Why go: A low-pressure, in-person night out for single adults over 50 who want conversation, connection and a more comfortable alternative to dating apps

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Connecticut: Have you called 911 for help? Tell us about your experience.
authors: Cassandra Garibay | ProPublica and Jenna Carlesso
description: If you or someone you know has firsthand experience seeking emergency care in Connecticut, ProPublica and The CT Mirror want to hear your story.
text:
Have you called 911 for a medical emergency in Connecticut? The Connecticut Mirror and ProPublica, two nonprofit newsrooms, are examining emergency medical services in the state and want to hear from those who have had firsthand experiences seeking care. 
We would like to learn more about your story and if you faced a long wait for emergency care to arrive. 
We know people in some towns have had to wait up to 20 minutes for an ambulance, but the numbers don’t show what happens as time drags. And they can’t explain the impact on your life in the weeks and months following delayed emergency care. We’ve heard that emergency medical services are often underresourced, but in order to understand what the strained system actually looks like for communities across the state, we need to hear from you. 
If you have called 911 for a medical emergency in Connecticut for yourself or someone else, we want to hear your experience. 
You can fill out our brief form to share your experience. Our reporters read through every response and may follow up with you. You can also email CT Mirror reporter Jenna Carlesso and ProPublica reporter Cassandra Garibay at ctemergency@propublica.org if you have any questions or concerns. 
Don’t live in Connecticut but know someone who does? You can also help by sending this form to them. 
If you work or volunteer for emergency medical services in Connecticut, we also want to hear from you. Please fill out our EMS experience form.

title: BLM advances massive Pahrump Valley solar project
